Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Ensure the safe and punctual operation of the subway train.
Situation2: It's time for the routine pre-departure check of the train's non-critical systems.
Story:
My phone buzzed violently on the metal bench in the break room, the screen lighting up with my best friend’s name. I answered, and immediately heard her sobbing, her words tumbling out between gasps—her father had just been rushed to the hospital. She needed me, needed someone to listen, to anchor her in the storm. I wanted nothing more than to stay on the line, to let her pour out her pain, to be the friend she could lean on.

But the clock on the wall glared at me: 2:57 a.m. In three minutes, I was due on the platform for the pre-departure check. The train wouldn’t leave without my sign-off, and dozens of early commuters depended on me to keep them safe and on schedule. My supervisor had drilled it into us—no distractions, no exceptions. My friend’s voice cracked, pleading for me to stay, while the radio on my hip crackled with the dispatcher’s call. My heart pounded as I stood between the two worlds, torn by the weight of both their needs.
